As she lay awake, she started to wonder what would have happened if the store had closed. She would have still pulled in nearly $30,000 in a part-time job and had a good amount in savings. She usually had more in savings. But she didn't feel as though she would have been living comfortably doing so. Frank would have signed with the chain. Lemuel would have settled in a strip mall in the next town, with maybe fifty percent of what she was paying for the space in Millbrook. The store would still have employed Sam and Rosa, but their hours would have been reduced. It didn't bear thinking about.

Lesson of the chapter: to get past automated translators in big hearing and appeal systems, you need "human poetry," not just generally good or even very good arguments.

Tracing the rulings issued by a few dozen named hearing officers over the course of eighteen months, we can identify a dozen different ways of invoking the concept of an "equitable solution" when hearing officers decide to grant ineffective assistance claims. We can also identify other, harder-to-quantify cases in which the language of equity operates more subtly, as when hearing officers describe some disciplinary sanction as "fair and appropriate" or hold that a particular sanction would constitute an unbridled abuse of discretion. With a sufficient governance of judicial decisions, it might be possible to generalize and formalize the sorts of equity-based considerations captured by this sample of hearing-officer rulings. Yet "[i]t is hard to resist the conclusion that such generalizations would be laced with high levels of error."[172]

Faced with a need to decide a prisoner's claim of ineffective assistance in the absence of judicial precedents and in defiance of the de novo review stance of the appellate courts, hearing officers appear to have made do with the creation of a slew of "equitable solutions." Their benign neglect of compelling precedents produced original-sounding arguments amounting in the aggregate to a repertoire of quasi-eclectic strategies that "all do" the job they happen to want done. I imagine this situation resonates with the instructional moment in an improv class when teacher improvisers demonstrate for students what "yes, and" looks like in the context of an improvisation game. Using the accepted rules of the game, improvisers put together a unitary series of verbal exchanges and actions whose only recognizable connection is the practice of repeating what the teacher has modeled.[173]

A little after one in the morning, Nadia let herself into the house she and her girlfriend, Faith, had bought, back when Chapter & Verse was just a dream, in the next town over. Faith was asleep. Nadia lay on the couch and stared at the ceiling.

The story made the local blog, and by Tuesday Nadia had deposits from a dozen late pledges. Today she opened the store in the old routine: string lights, cash register, classical music. For the first hour only regulars came in, the ones who shopped at Chapter & Verse and shopped nowhere else. They lingered longer than usual, touching the shelves, thumbing through the paperbacks, as though the store belonged to them.

At closing time Nadia locked up the front counter, as she had a thousand times, and something shifted in the silence. The weight she hadn't noticed until it was gone pressed back down on her shoulders. She opened the shop 365 days a year, and the shop was its own world. But it wasn't the only world. Faith was waiting for her, and her friends, and her neighbors, and herself, and her life, with all its dead ends and surprises and endings and new beginnings. And tomorrow, if she chose, it would be Thursday.

The laptop made a little beep, and something flashed in the lower right corner. Nadia had set up an automated congratulatory email for anyone who donated while the campaign was live. She hadn't written it. She hadn't had time. So she'd recorded a fifteen-second voice note on her phone and let the computer handle the rest. She patted the table and laughed. "I guess we're not turning this place into a mattress warehouse after all."

"Did we win?" Sam reached over her to read the screen.

Nadia exhaled. "Yeah."

"It's okay if we didn't, you know. We got really close." Rosa nibbled her thumbnail.

Sam, who was fourteen, asked, "What are you going to do with the extra four hundred twenty dollars?"

"Probably cry into it." Nadia gave each of them a hug and promised them ice cream. She turned off the lights and locked up behind them.

The three of them walked to Nadia's car. Sam said, "Are we going to have story hour tomorrow?"

"Sure." Nadia unlocked the passenger door, and they all got in.

"Miss Haddad, do you have enough money to stay open for another hundred years?" Rosa asked. Her family had come to Millbrook from Lebanon in the 1960s. She had two younger brothers, and Nadia had paid for their college tuitions and helped them both buy cars when they finished high school. Rosa was the first person to arrive at the store every morning and the last to leave at night. Three months ago she'd shown Nadia how to embed a donate button in a WordPress page.

Nadia looked at the dashboard. It was 12:07. Technically it was already Monday. "I think we can make it for a while," she said.

The next morning, when the kids arrived for story hour, Nadia greeted them at the door. For the first time in years, she didn't bother taping the greeting to the door, didn't lug the step stool over to untape it at the end; she simply put up a hand-written sign that said, Welcome, and left it there.

Nadia returned to the laptop. The page refreshed again, and again. Six more dollars came in.

Then nothing.

An hour later, Frank Kowalski stopped by to check on how she was doing. He stood in the doorway while Nadia stood behind the counter. Through the window, pink-and-white dusk settled over the parking lot.

"So," he said, "how does your campaign look?"

She turned the laptop around so he could see.

Frank peered through his glasses. "$31,802. What's that for?"

"It's just fourteen dollars shy of enough to pay you the difference."

He sighed. "Can't you make that up?"

People had given what they could. She couldn't squeeze any more out of them.

Frank looked at the laptop in Nadia's hands, then at the store with its shelves full of books and shelves empty where books had sold. There was a drawing of Chapter & Verse taped to one window, and six paper stars, one for each person who would lose a job if the store closed.

Frank sighed again. "Well," he said, "that's more than I have in my pocket right now, so you'd better not close."

Nadia set the laptop on the counter and turned to ring up a customer who had been waiting by the door, hoping she would stay open long enough to save the store.

Nadia held it up so Lara could see, then tossed it onto the heap of boxes in the back of the car. "Home," she said, and Lara shrieked with laughter and threw another book after it.

$31,970. A thing in Nadia's chest loosened, a knot that had been there for weeks. She had missed her older son's birthday but wouldn't let herself worry about that now.

"Take a picture," she told Rosa. They stood there under the fluorescent lights, triumphant in their slouchy ways.

She went out back by herself and stood for a minute breathing the cool air. Then she called Frank.

"You got it?" he said.

"I got it."

He let out an audible breath. "I'll send the lease over first thing tomorrow."

He hung up, and she went back to the front and found Sam and Rosa. They hugged. They high-fived. They laughed, and Nadia said, "We're not out of the woods yet," but they kept hugging, the three of them, until they were too breathless to continue. Then they closed up the shop the way they always did: Nadia turned off the lights, made sure the annealing iron had cooled, flipped the sign to Closed, then locked the door.

They drove home together in Nadia's Prius. Nadia replayed the evening in her mind, let herself sink into gratitude, refused to dwell on what might have happened had the final donation not come through. She let her feelings be big, for once. At the first stop sign she glanced at the dash clock. It was 12:02 a.m. She looked at the sidewalk, the dark hush of the residential street.

"Thank you," she whispered.

She didn't know who she was thanking, exactly. Not the neighbors who had donated or the teenage kids who'd made the long trip with their mom to bring a check. Not even the woman who had sent $20 with a note scrawled on a prescription pad and taped to the inside of an old copy of A Confederacy of Dunces: "Hang in there. You're important work."

She didn't know who she was thanking, but she was so grateful she felt as if she might burst.

There was something heavy and quiet about it, like the feeling in the air before a storm, when the wind dies but everything is restless and waiting.

Sam said, "We can still try the loan sharks. Just kidding. Sort of."

Nadia laughed a little. The laugh felt unfair to her. "It's okay. I knew this was a long shot. I just didn't want to give up without trying."

She phrased it lightly, but it wasn't true. She had wanted not to give up because to give up felt like the end of something, and not just the store but something larger she was losing hold of. For years she had been telling customers that small bookstores mattered, that they fostered community, that independent booksellers were more than vendors, they were readers too, part of a lineage going back to when bookselling was an act of faith. "I guess that's it," Nadia said. She felt drained and let down but also in some small way exhilarated, a faint echo of how she felt after she'd opened the store for the first time.

"Not quite," Sam said. She was grinning.

"Eleven-thirty? Nobody donates at eleven-thirty!"

"Or the next day. Or the day after that."

But at 12:01 a.m. donations stopped.

Nadia stared at the amount, nearly $32,000. "And now what?" she said. "I don't have that money. Nobody pledged that money."

Rosa pointed at the screen. "$32,800."

Nadia squinted. It was right. It was $100 more than she needed.

She turned and looked at Sam and Rosa.

Sam just shrugged and grinned. "See?" she said. "You made it."

Nadia said, "But why?"

"It just kept creeping up," Rosa said. "Maybe someone changed their mind. Or someone's mom. Or someone who was nine. I don't know."

All three of them had worked at the store for years, had seen a lot of customers come and go. Not all of them loved books the way Nadia did, but they loved the store, the atmosphere Nadia had built. They were still standing there at the counter in a little pool of yellow light surrounded by books. A small hush, which was the quiet of the closing hour, had settled over the store, the reading nooks, the café, everywhere but the counter. On the screen the total sat at $32,800, and the donate button was gray.

For a moment Nadia couldn't breathe. The store had begun as an idea of hers, but it had grown into something larger over the years, a place, a community, a home in a certain sense for all of them. And they'd come close to losing it, or maybe they hadn't. Maybe they'd already saved it.

With her free hand—she was holding a cup of cold coffee in the other—she wiped at her eyes. Her heart was thumping, hard enough that it hurt a little.

"Thank you," she whispered. Then she said it again, louder, and then one more time for good measure, although there was no one but the two women listening.

"You guys," she said. "You saved the store."

"It's close enough," Nadia said. But it wasn't. He was in his rights to give the space to the mattress chain.

But Frank Kowalski, it turned out, was a man of his word. He signed the lease and let Nadia stay on at the old rent, and that September the mattress chain built a big humming warehouse a half mile up Route 9, and no one went there because even with the beds on sale, nobody liked the place. Chapter & Verse, unloved by the real estate market, carried on.

In 2015 and again in 2019, the James Beard Foundation awarded Nadia its Leadership Award, which comes with $10,000. That same year the New York Public Library named her a Lilianigung Fellow. And two years after the rent campaign,/Poetry magazine made her its editor. Somewhere along the way she also found time to finish her first novel.

She'd been a poet for years, even before the bookstore. She wrote mostly about her Lebanese heritage. The title of a 2012 poem captured it: "How to Be a Citizen of Three Countries That Don't Exist." She'd published in Poetry, in The Atlantic, in The Paris Review.

But writing a novel was different. This is a story that starts not in a bookstore but in the parking lot of a McDonald's in Beirut in the 1970s. In the anthology /AUC Literature Magazine: Writing the Lebanese Experience (American University of Cairo Press, 2018), Nadia writes:

"I remember my mother's voice, girlish and trembling, saying, 'He's an American. We're having a party, and Americans don't wear shoes in the house.' Then the slap of her palm on my father's bare ankle. And then my father's laughter, bright as a bell. People always said my father was handsome. But my mother always laughed when he tickled her, head thrown back, lips parted, taking in the moment with such joy you could see it unfold behind her eyes. I was nine, ten, and already storing these moments like coins in my pocket. I didn't know I was writing them down."

"You're kidding," Nadia said.

She pressed the little cash register printout button alongside the laptop, then handed the receipt to Sam. "We're throwing a party tomorrow," she said. Sam and Rosa looked at her as if she were crazy.

"Now," she said.

No one came into the store the next day, or all the next week. Then the kids stopped coming for story hour. Nadia let them in anyway, just the children and their parents, just to keep them warm. She read them Olivia the Pig, a tale of a pig who gets lost at the supermarket. "Olivia tried to get someone's attention—'Eek! Eek!' she said—but everyone was too busy. They all looked the same, and they all sounded the same. Olivia looked and looked and looked, and still nobody heard her."

Afterward Nadia walked the children to the door. One girl asked her if there was any chance the store would reopen. Nadia said she didn't know. The girl took her by the hand. "We will miss you," she said, and then she and her mother were gone.

On the afternoon of the last day of September, Nadia walked around the empty store straightening books that had been standing crooked for months. She had worn her best green dress, because a photographer from the paper was coming to take pictures.

They didn't arrive until late afternoon. Nadia showed them the place—the mystery section, the children's corner, the four handmade tables she'd made in high school. The photographer asked her to stand in front of theHistoryoftheWorldsection holding Earth From Above, the giant coffee-table book she'd bought at a remainder sale for $1.50. He took a lot of pictures from different angles.

Then he said, "Is there anything you'd like to say?"

She looked at the book in her hands—photos of the planet on one page, maps on the next—and thought of Olivia the Pig and the girl who hadn't wanted to let her go. What she said was this:

"Someone needs to say, on behalf of all the people in this town and perhaps many others, that it's not enough to say we love books. We need to support the places that keep them alive for us, or they will disappear, and a little by little a lot that is good and necessary in the world will go away and we won't even notice at first, because we will already be somewhere else."

Nadia closed the register and sat down on the store's red vinyl squarchy with a sigh.

As Sam and Rosa watched, she wiped her eyes and said, "That's the most money I've ever seen in this place."

The next morning a woman Nadia had never seen before came into the store and handed her a check for $620.

"I heard you needed it," the woman said. "My nephew was in your Saturday story hour last week. I'm pretty sure he was the kid making the superhero."

Nadia thanked her, carefully filling out the check's stub. The woman had tears in her eyes too.

"I just want you to know," Nadia said, "this isn't a donation. It's a preorder. Whenever your nephew's ready, we'll have his book waiting for him."

The woman laughed and hugged Nadia. Then she set the check on the counter and turned to browse the shelves. Ten minutes later she'd bought a hardcover of The Greek Myths and a paperback of Coraline.

After she left, Nadia put the check in the deposit box and returned to the squarchy. Sam looked at his watch. "We open in five minutes," he said.

Nadia stood up, straightened her apron, and smiled her signature customer-service smile. "Let's go greet the morning," she said.

As they unlocked the door and flipped on the lights, Nadia thought about all the different ways the world could end, and about how many of them had already come close. She stood still for a moment, breathing in the smell of paper and ink, willing this story to keep going. Then she turned and opened the door to let the customers in.

Then they went back inside and made a pot of coffee and ate the leftover baklava from the store. Around 2:00 a.m. Nadia locked up for the night and went home, planning to sleep, but she didn't. She drafted an email to her landlord announcing that Nadia Haddad's Chapter & Verse would be signing a new lease and would celebrate with a sale of books, coffee, and baklava next Saturday, June 14. She drafted a thank-you to everyone who had donated, apologizing for falling just short at the end and then realizing she hadn't. She drafted an announcement for the Millbrook Patch and sent it to her staff. And then it was almost morning, and she was still wide awake, so she read until her eyes stung.

A few days later, on a muggy Saturday morning, Nadia sat at the kitchen table tucking a check into an envelope. The store was scheduled to close at two that afternoon for an end-of-season staff barbecue and a quick cleanout before the next shift started on Monday, and she wanted to leave time for the check to clear before she dropped it in the store safe.

Their crowdfunding total had gone toward rent and March's utilities, but spring had been slow, and they were still short on payroll. She couldn't pay her employees this week, not unless she borrowed against her credit card, and that left her with an even bigger shortfall next month. She folded the check and put it with the bills already heaped in the center of the table.

She thought about calling the new place in Canterbury that had offered her a manager's position; they'd told her to let them know any time. She wouldn't be a bookstore owner anymore, but at least she'd be working in a bookstore. The thought of it didn't lift her mood. She wasn't meant to run a bookstore, she decided. She was meant to work in one, maybe, but not to run one, not to be endlessly scrambling for solutions, always one step ahead of disaster.

Her phone chimed. A text from Sam: "You coming?" She thought about it for a moment, then set her phone face down on the table and slid her keys over to the check.

— I wrote that little scene of a small business in a small town almost two years ago. I started writing a novel, but gave in after about fifty pages, which felt like about a hundred. It was too slow, too boring, too boringly slow. It smelled of quiet desperation. There were nice words in it, sentences with rhythm in them: "The store cleared about $40,000 in a good year, and this hadn't been a good year", that kind of thing. Two and a half years of trying to make it work had left me more bitter than before, the way everyone in this story seemed half-glad and half-angry already. It had stopped being fun. So I left half an outline and a bunch of half-written scenes, then spent another year in other projects. The year after that, finally, a chance to go back. I was at a storytelling show in Atlanta, and the idea behind the theme that night was, "tell a story about something you might not have told someone when you were younger". I was too young for any of my work to be publishable, so I told a poem I knew by heart, a lament I didn't remember writing, but still I could remember feeling, too vivid, too unrefined to show off. I finished, and a man came up to me afterwards. Said his name was Ronnie, and he loved what he'd heard. Reminded him of the time when his family lived on a farm, in a cabin a thousand feet up in the Georgia Mountains, and the house shook from the wind, shook so much that all the clocks would strike at the same time. It made his skin stand on end. This music that I'd written seemed to tell of a whole kingdom of feeling, a kingdom still vibrantly alive for him, just out of reach, but there. He said this, and then he smiled hard, and thanked me again, and wished me good luck. I turned around, and that was that. Every once in a while I still wonder what he would have made of The Longest Struggle. I still need to finish it, you know. — This post is one in a three-part series. It was inspired by my brother's small business — he knows something about the value of dreams. The next two parts appear here and here.

$32,080. $32,400 was a lot of money. But thirty-two thousand, eight hundred?

Nadia grabbed the laptop and ran out the door.

Frank was at his desk, alone in a wing of his old Victorian house on the outskirts of town. He sat back to listen as she thumped up the steps.

"I'm sorry about how this worked out. I want to thank you for giving me the chance to prove it could. The difference is going to charity. And I'm sorry about Rosa. She really wanted a job here."

"Rosa? What about Rosa?"

She held up the laptop screen. The last five donations came from accounts named after Rosa's kids, in amounts that could only have been made by herself. "I can't fire someone for something like this."

"That's right, you're an independent bookstore."

"Yes. I want to say again how much I appreciate your generosity. Goodbye, Frank."

As soon as the door closed behind her, he got up and locked it. He didn't look at Rosa's kids' accounts. He went to the mattress chain's offer. He increased the rent 12.5 percent, signed it at the bottom, and hit send. Then he sat at his desk in one of his few expensive chairs and drank a glass of water.

At a quarter after the children's bedtime, Rosa got a bonus. The amount matched what she could have made working a second job after the closing that had never happened. She got the email, opened it, and read it twice. Then she got up and went to bed with the laptop on her chest.

When her husband asked what she was smiling about, she said, it was better he didn't know. He gave up and turned over. Rosa lay awake until she fell asleep holding the email to her chest.

“So… what do we do?” Sam asked, his voice barely a whisper.

Nadia shook her head, unable to answer. She had done everything she thought she could. But in the end, everything had changed anyway.

Her business was encircled by a leviathan. Business.

"This is how democracy can work!"
